H1.text: A door swings on its hinge. A fan blade spins on its axle. A wheel turns on a bicycle. Nothing breaks. Only the position changes.

H2.text: Molecules can do this too. In ethane, the single bond between the two carbons is the axle.

H3.text: Aarav spins the front wheel of his bicycle in the college corridor. The spokes keep passing the fork.

H4.text: One moment a spoke hides right behind the fork. The next moment it sits in a gap.

H5.text: By the end, you will know why ethane prefers one way of sitting, and by how much.

P2.text: In ethane, two carbons are joined by one sigma bond. Each carbon also holds three hydrogens.

P3.text: A sigma bond is like an axle. One carbon can spin, and the bond does not break.

P4.text: Each new arrangement made by this spin is called a conformation.

P5.text: There are endless conformations. Two are special. In the eclipsed form, the back hydrogens hide right behind the front ones.

P6.text: In the staggered form, the back hydrogens sit in the gaps between the front ones.

S1.text: How do we draw this on paper? There are two ways. First, the sawhorse projection.

S2.text: Look at the carbon carbon bond from an angle. Draw it as a long slanted line. The front carbon sits at the lower end, the back carbon at the upper end.

S3.text: Each carbon carries three hydrogens, drawn as short lines.

S4.text: Second, the Newman projection. Now look straight down the carbon carbon bond, head on.

S5.text: The front carbon is a point. Its three bonds meet at the centre.

S6.text: The back carbon hides behind it, so we draw it as a circle. Its bonds start at the edge of the circle.

S7.text: Now spin the back carbon. Watch closely. Every sixty degrees, the molecule switches between eclipsed and staggered.

B1.text: Which form is more stable? Think of the bonds as clouds of electrons.

B2.text: In the eclipsed form, the bond clouds of the front and back face each other, like two crowds meeting in a narrow corridor. They push.

B3.text: In the staggered form, the clouds sit as far apart as they can. Less push.

B4.text: Pause and think. Which form has the lower energy, eclipsed or staggered?

B5.text: Staggered! Its bond clouds are farthest apart, so it has the least push, the lowest energy, and the most stability.

D1.text: Let's measure this push, link by link.

D2.text: Link one. The push between the bond clouds of the two carbons is called torsional strain.

D3.text: Link two. The eclipsed form has the most torsional strain, so it has the highest energy. The staggered form has the least.

D4.text: Link three. Plot the energy as the back carbon turns. The curve rises and falls every sixty degrees, like hills and valleys.

D5.text: Link four. The height of each hill is only about twelve point five kilojoules per mole. This is the energy barrier to rotation.

D6.text: Link five. This barrier is tiny. At room temperature, molecules bump into each other hard enough to cross it all the time. So we cannot separate the two forms.

T1.text: Remember this. Same bonds, different spin. Staggered is the comfortable seat.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. In one full turn of the back carbon, how many eclipsed and staggered forms appear, and what does climbing the hills cost?

W2.text: Step one. The angle between a front bond and a back bond, in the Newman view, is called the dihedral angle.

W3.text: Step two. Eclipsed forms come at zero, one hundred and twenty, and two hundred and forty degrees.

W4.text: Step three. Staggered forms come at sixty, one hundred and eighty, and three hundred degrees. So, three of each in one turn.

W5.text: Step four. Each climb from staggered to eclipsed costs twelve point five kilojoules per mole. For two moles, that is twenty five kilojoules.

W6.text: Every form in between, neither eclipsed nor staggered, is called a skew form.

C1.text: Now put the two drawings side by side.

C2.text: The sawhorse shows the bond from the side, so you can see both carbons and the length of the bond.

C3.text: The Newman view looks down the bond, so you see the angle between front and back bonds at a glance.

C4.text: Same molecule, same form. Only the camera angle changes.

X2.text: Students write that rotation about the carbon carbon single bond in ethane is completely free.

X3.text: Wrong. It is almost free, but not completely. A small barrier of about twelve point five kilojoules per mole stands in the way.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Board papers ask you to draw the sawhorse and Newman projections. Entrance tests ask about stability and torsional strain.

Q1.text: Exam level now. In a Newman projection of ethane, the back carbon starts eclipsed and turns by one hundred and eighty degrees. What do we get? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Staggered, at the lowest energy.

A2.text: Eclipsed forms come every one hundred and twenty degrees: at zero, one twenty and two forty.

A3.text: One hundred and eighty is not on that list. It sits halfway between one twenty and two forty, so it is staggered.

A4.text: Staggered is the lowest point on the curve, twelve point five kilojoules per mole below eclipsed. A and D get the form wrong, and C is a skew form.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. In a Newman projection, how is the back carbon drawn?

Y3.text: Two. Why is the staggered form more stable than the eclipsed form?

Y4.text: Three. Why can we not separate the two forms of ethane in a bottle?

N1.text: Next time: why can a double bond not spin like a single bond? We find out in alkenes, their structure, isomerism and preparation.
